newsitem.title: USA: Clinton wins corporate nod, visits New Hampshire.
newsitem.headline: Clinton wins corporate nod, visits New Hampshire.

text.p: One day after debating Republican Bob Dole, President Bill Clinton on Monday courted his opponent's core constituencies, winning an endorsement from big business and campaigning in conservative New Hampshire.

At a morning speech in Stamford, Connecticut, Clinton appeared with the chief executives of several large U.S. companies, including Sprint, Xerox and United Technologies, all of whom praised him as good for big business.

The Clinton/Gore campaign said the men were among more than 2,500 "business leaders" who had decided to endorse the president and argued that their support vindicated Clinton's management of the economy.
The endorsement was unusual in U.S. politics, where industry has typically sided with the Republicans rather than the Democrats.
But many executives on the list have long supported Clinton while others, like Tom Horan of Connecticut's Horan Florists did not appear to be titans of the business world.

"I have wondered through the years why the Democratic Party should not have at least as much or more support from American business as the other party," Clinton told about 500 businessmen and women at Stamford's Rich Forum theatre.
"We never thought that ... helping ordinary people live up to their full potential was inconsistent with trying to build a strong business environment," he added.

Clinton and his aides used the endorsements to argue that Dole's natural allies were deserting him. National opinion polls show Clinton leads Dole by 10 to 20 percentage points ahead of the Nov. 5 election.

"There is a problem developing in their ranks ... about traditional sources of Republican support drying up," said White House spokesman Mike McCurry. "Having such a show of support for the president ... has got to be a little dispiriting for them."
White House political director Doug Sosnik made a similar argument for the president's afternoon trip to Manchester, New Hampshire, saying the state had swung to Clinton.

A Mason-Dixon poll published last month showed Clinton beating Dole in New Hampshire by 49 to 38 percent, with independent Ross Perot at five percent. Sosnik said more recent polls put Clinton ahead by more than 20 points.
Clinton won the state in 1992, but, in a demonstration of its conservative roots, did so with a margin of only 6,500 votes.
At a boisterous outdoor rally in Manchester, Clinton reminded the crowd of several thousand that he had first declared his candidacy for president five years ago to the day in New Hampshire.
"There may be someone in America right now who's happier than I am but I have no idea who it would be. I am glad to be here," Clinton said.
Clinton also said he was pleased with Sunday night's debate against Dole in Hartford, Connecticut.

"I enjoyed that debate and I believe that the American people got a pretty good feel for the differences between us," Clinton said. "We just proved you can still do it and be civilised and decent and humane."
Clinton was later scheduled to visit Portland, Maine for a nighttime rally before flying back to Washington early on Tuesday.
